query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten‐based refractory alloys for fusion plasma-facing components, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by diffusion-assisted dislocation climb occurring at the grain boundaries. By doping the grain boundaries to reduce their diffusivity, the rate of dislocation climb is suppressed, leading to a measurable reduction in plastic strain under high-temperature stress (with a possible concomitant change in strain hardening and toughness) compared to an unperturbed alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated tungsten-based refractory alloy with baseline grain-boundary chemistry and microstructure typical for plasma-facing applications.
generation.intervention: Tailored grain-boundary doping (e.g., with a small, segregating dopant known to increase grain-boundary cohesion and lower diffusivity) while keeping the bulk composition and grain size constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature, diffusion-activated regime (e.g., 600–800 °C) under mechanical loading conditions simulating fusion reactor service; experiments conducted under identical strain rates for both doped and undoped samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified grain-boundary diffusivity due to dopant segregation, which alters the ease of dislocation climb across grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, atomic diffusion along grain boundaries enables dislocation climb that accommodates plastic deformation. Dopant atoms segregated to grain boundaries reduce local diffusivity and hence impede dislocation climb. This modification suppresses plastic strain (and alters strain hardening behavior and toughness) relative to that observed in the baseline material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature mechanical loading, the doped (grain-boundary engineered) sample will exhibit lower plastic strain rates (and higher yield strength) versus the baseline. There may be slight changes in strain hardening and toughness if reduced dislocation climb alters the balance between ductility and strength.
generation.baseline: An undoped tungsten-based refractory alloy with unmodified grain-boundary chemistry.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic relationship is expected to hold for materials operating in the diffusion-activated high-temperature regime (below melting) and for alloys whose grain size and microstructural features remain similar aside from the targeted grain-boundary chemistry modification.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the effect and the balance between reduced plastic strain and possible changes in toughness depend on the choice and concentration of the dopant, as well as precise processing conditions. Quantitative predictions require further parameter calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory alloy samples with identical processing routes and microstructural characteristics: one set with added grain-boundary dopants and one undoped control. Subject both sets to high-temperature (600–800 °C) mechanical tests (e.g., creep or constant-load tensile tests) under identical strain rate conditions. Precisely measure yield strength, plastic strain rate, and strain hardening behavior.
measurements: Plastic strain rate under a given load
Total plastic strain at fixed time intervals
Microstructural analysis (grain-boundary chemistry and possible dopant segregation verification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in plastic strain rate or an increase in yield strength relative to the undoped baseline, or if the dopant addition fails to alter the grain-boundary chemistry as verified by microanalysis, then the hypothesis that diffusion-assisted dislocation climb governs high-temperature deformation via grain-boundary diffusivity modulation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As can be seen from the results in Summary I confirm 3.2 of this paper, obvious grain boundary slip occurs in the high-entropy alloy at high temperatures. Due to the high temperature, the thermal motion of atoms is intensified, and a large number of disordered atoms are formed from the original position of atoms, and these disordered atoms are mostly concentrated near the crystallization, as shown in Figure 7c,d. At low temperatures, this phenomenon is not obvious, and no large number of disordered atoms are produced, as shown in Figure 7a,b. However, at low temperatures, a large number of dislocations are generated, which slip within the grain and gather and intertwine at the grain boundaries to form dislocation knots, as shown in Figure 7e,f. The strain rate has a great influence on dislocation. By comparing Figure 7e,f (or Figure 7g,h), it can be found that more dislocations and entanglement occur at higher strain rates. Therefore, at high temperatures, grain boundary slip is more serious and plays a leading role in deformation. How the grain boundary affects the deformation behaviour and thus improves the mechanical properties of HEAs becomes a primary question for researchers. In previous work, Yu et al. observed that a CrFeCoNiPd alloy had higher continuous steady strain hardening than that in other single-phase HEAs with similar grain sizes at ambient temperature. They also hypothesized that plastic deformation at room temperature was primarily involved in the 1/2 <110> {111} full dislocation. Lu et al. simulated the deposition and annealing process of AlCoCrCuFeNi HEAs and observed that a phase of the cluster structure was transformed from BCC to FCC. The clustering in HEAs has a significant effect on the phase transition. Huang et al. simulated the glass transition temperature of Al–Cu–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs using molecular dynamics (MD). Li et al. simulated the structural transformation process of a AlCrCoCuFeNi HEA at different cooling rates by molecular dynamics. Few studies have focused on the influence of the grain boundary on the strength of high entropy alloys. frame.system: Structural materials for fusion plasma‐facing components (e.g., tungsten-based or refractory alloys) in their as‐fabricated microstructures and compositions, designed to operate under extreme high-temperature and radiation conditions.
frame.goal: To identify and validate a single mechanistic hypothesis that explains the governing process behind high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in these materials.
frame.limitation: Current understanding lacks a unified, testable mechanism that isolates the dominant deformation process at high temperatures; previous models have not conclusively distinguished the contributions of different microstructural mechanisms (like dislocation glide, climb, or grain-boundary sliding) in the complex fusion environment.
constraints: Must be testable via controlled experiments that isolate one mechanistic factor from other variables
The hypothesis needs to specify quantitative predictions relative to an unmodified (baseline) specimen
Defined boundaries of applicability (e.g., a specific temperature range and microstructural state)
The comparison must account for variables such as grain boundary chemistry, defect density, and solute segregation
Prior evidence from high-temperature deformation studies must be acknowledged.
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions (in a diffusion-activated regime but below melting) under mechanical stress levels mimicking service conditions in fusion reactors, where diffusion-based processes (e.g., dislocation climb assisted by grain-boundary diffusion) become prominent.
prior_attempts: Prior studies have separately examined contributions from dislocation glide vs. grain-boundary sliding and attempted to link creep rates to overall toughness, but they did not isolate the dominant mechanism through controlled modifications of grain-boundary properties.

Existing creep and high-temperature deformation experiments in refractory metals and steels provide indirect evidence of diffusion‐activated dislocation climb, yet they have not explicitly tested the role of grain-boundary mediated processes under isolated conditions.
